name: Bryter Layter
editorial_article: Released in November 1970, Bryter Layter serves as the second studio album by the enigmatic English singer-songwriter Nick Drake. While his debut, Five Leaves Left, introduced the world to his hushed, melancholic folk style, Bryter Layter arrived as a more polished and instrumentally ambitious work. Produced once again by Joe Boyd, the album famously moved away from the singular folk intimacy of his predecessor, embracing a sophisticated, baroque pop sound enriched by the precise orchestral arrangements of Robert Kirby. \n\nCentral to the album's distinct character are the contributions of John Cale, formerly of The Velvet Underground. Cale lent his multi-instrumental talents—including piano, celeste, and organ—to pivotal tracks such as the sublime "Northern Sky," providing a warm, melodic counterpoint to Drake’s delicate guitar picking and introspective songwriting. The ensemble also featured members of the Fairport Convention, specifically bassist Dave Pegg and drummer Dave Mattacks, whose involvement helped ground the arrangements in a light, jazzy folk-rock groove. Despite the inclusion of these broader musical textures, the album remains fundamentally centered on Drake's poetic, yearning voice and intricate, idiosyncratic acoustic guitar tunings. Though it struggled commercially upon release, Bryter Layter is now widely regarded as one of the most influential and beautiful records of the era, standing as a masterclass in the balance between singer-songwriter vulnerability and high-level studio production. It remains a definitive document of the late 60s British folk-rock sound, offering a lighter, more playful—yet still deeply melancholic—alternative to the folk traditions of the time.

editorial_pitch: Bryter Layter is the sophisticated, jazz-inflected second album from English singer-songwriter Nick Drake, featuring intricate arrangements by Robert Kirby and guest contributions from John Cale. It captures a more expansive, colorful sound compared to the sparse intimacy of his debut, establishing itself as a pinnacle of the late 1960s British folk-rock movement.
